item.title: When Is Prosocial Behavior Intuitive? The Moderating Role of Empathic Perspective Taking
item.description: arXiv:2611.10155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Why is prosocial behavior intuitive for some individuals but deliberative for others? We examine whether empathic perspective taking moderates the association between reflective processing and prosocial choice. We run a laboratory experiment with 652 participants, where we measure prosociality using a four-player Distribution Game that holds aggregate payoffs constant and orders allocations from self-regarding to egalitarian. We combine participants' choices with the Perspective Taking subscale of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index, a five-item Cognitive Reflection Test, and choice-stage response time in the allocation decision. Perspective taking significantly moderates the association between response time and prosociality. At high levels of perspective taking, longer response times are associated with modestly lower prosociality; at low levels, the association is positive but not statistically significant. No comparable moderation emerges for Cognitive Reflection Test performance. These results are consistent with the possibility that, when others' outcomes are readily represented (high perspective taking), prosocial choices may arise relatively quickly, while additional decision-specific processing may be associated with greater attention to their private cost. When others' outcomes are less salient (low perspective taking), additional processing may instead help bring them into consideration. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing processing proximal to the specific decision from domain-general analytic reflection when explaining whether prosocial behavior appears intuitive.
item.dc:creator: Enrico D'Ecclesiis, Francesca Pancotto, Barbara Luppi, Simone Righi

item.title: Have wind and solar energy increased electricity price volatility? And what is electricity price volatility, anyway?
item.description: arXiv:2611.10731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is widely held that wind and solar power increase the volatility of electricity prices. This paper argues that the literature conflates two distinct types of price variation: across delivery time and across trading time. Determined simultaneously in the same day-ahead auction, prices for power to be delivered in distinct quarter-hours differ. This price dispersion, which I call "variability," is rooted in non-storability. After that auction, trading continues in intraday markets until imbalance settlement. The price for the same delivery period changes as new information arises, such as updated weather forecasts. This price "volatility" is ultimately caused by uncertainty. This paper develops a simple algebraic model of day-ahead and imbalance markets that provides a formal definition of variability and volatility, allows for their decomposition, and derives their fundamental drivers: uncertainty and non-storability. It then presents empirical data on price variability and volatility in Germany over the past 25 years, during which the share of wind and solar energy increased from zero to nearly 50% of generation. Variability followed a U-shaped trajectory, falling from the 2000s to the 2010s before increasing again. Volatility, in contrast, declined over time.
item.dc:creator: Lion Hirth

item.title: The Effect of the U.S. Federal Production Tax Credit on Negative Energy Prices
item.description: arXiv:2611.11112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Negative prices frequently arise in electricity markets and production subsidies are commonly cited as a leading cause. Using data from the U.S. Eastern Interconnection wholesale electricity markets for the period 2000-2023, we document that at least 18 percent of the total hours with negative energy prices cannot solely be attributed to the federal production tax credit (PTC), a large, persistent production subsidy during the period of study. Next, we provide the first causal evidence that the PTC leads to negative energy prices. On average, increasing PTC-eligible wind generation by 1 percent increases the probability of a negative energy price by 3.4 percentage points. However, significant heterogeneity exists across electricity markets, and some markets show an effect that is an order of magnitude larger. Furthermore, the PTC explains only 10 percent of the observed negative prices that could potentially be attributable to it. Finally, we use the causal estimate to calculate a plausible value for the environmental benefits accrued from the PTC subsidy when energy prices are negative.
item.dc:creator: Erik P. Johnson, Daniel H. Karney

item.title: Optimal power expansion planning under uncertainty in sub-Saharan Africa: A stochastic dual dynamic programming approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.11490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal electricity access and decarbonization are interlinked challenges for sub-Saharan Africa. Generation expansion planning methods used in the region rarely represent sequential and irreversible investment under demand and hydrological uncertainty. This paper develops a multistage stochastic generation expansion model solved with stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) to address the problem. The model represents demand and country-specific Markov hydrological uncertainty, accounts for technology-specific construction lead times, and endogenous reliability. The model is applied to the Ethiopia and Zimbabwe power systems over 2025--2050. The results show that for Ethiopia, the least-cost pathway is hydropower, with wind and solar sources providing increasing diversification. The model reduces cumulative expected unserved energy by about 78 TWh relative to a lower-cost deterministic expected value investment plan. For Zimbabwe, the least-cost pathway expands solar, hydropower, and gas while retaining residual coal as inherited coal capacity retires. Additionally, carbon pricing reduces emissions and increases resource costs by about 3\% to 5\%, creating a gradual cost-emissions trade-off. Combining a carbon tax policy with concessional solar financing renders the lowest average annual emissions while keeping resource costs below the baseline, which solves the model without emission constraint. At approximately matched expected emissions, emission caps have higher net resource costs than the corresponding carbon tax scenarios. The overall results imply that adaptive investment model can reduce power shortage exposure, while carbon policy design and lower clean investment costs shape the cost of decarbonization in developing power systems.
item.dc:creator: Arega Getaneh Abate, Xiao-Bing Zhang, Xiufeng Liu, Ruyu Liu, Per Sieverts Nielsen

item.title: Fairness Drift: Assessing Algorithmic Fairness in a Moving Market
item.description: arXiv:2611.11783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flexible models and richer data can reduce systematic valuation errors and improve fairness. Yet algorithmic values stay fixed between updates while the market moves, so a new algorithm gains most against an intact distortion and least where uneven appreciation has eroded or just reversed it. We study property assessment, which sets tax bills and has long over-assessed cheaper homes. Cook County replaced township regressions and manual adjustments with a gradient-boosted model and richer data on its triennial cycle: Chicago in 2021, northern suburbs in 2022, southern in 2023. We estimate difference-in-differences in how the assessment-to-price ratio varies with sale price and neighborhood minority share. In Chicago, the reform halved the relative over-assessment of cheaper homes and, among equally priced homes, weakened the link to neighborhood racial composition. In the suburbs the price gradient was unchanged: the North's legacy values were already accurate, and the South's cheap neighborhoods had appreciated faster under frozen values, correcting part of the distortion, then stalled in the reassessment year, leaving the new values too high where prices had gained and accuracy unimproved. Fairness thus drifts with the market between updates, and single-deployment evaluations may credit or blame the algorithm for what the market did.
item.dc:creator: Meng Liu

item.title: Does fare communication format matter? Evidence from a randomised experiment in public transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.12117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Highly concentrated demand in public transport places pressure on infrastructure and reduces service quality. Pricing instruments-such as discounted off-peak single fare tickets-are a widely used tool for rescheduling demand across time. Yet no study has directly examined whether the price communication format of single fare tickets affects travel behaviour in terms of departure-time rescheduling. To fill this gap, we exploit a randomised stated preference survey conducted in Switzerland based on participants' actual journeys (n = 1,082), assigning participants to one of three price formats: absolute amounts, absolute deviations, or percentage deviations from their current fare. Estimating a multinomial logit model with price-format interaction terms, we find no significant effect of communication format on aggregate price sensitivity. However, for low-fare trips, percentage-based communication substantially amplifies price sensitivity relative to absolute amounts or absolute deviations. Moreover, when prices are shown as percentage deviations, price sensitivity increases for small price spreads and decreases for large price spreads, with a crossover point corresponding to a discount depth of approximately 47%. In summary, these findings suggest that percentage-based price communication has the potential to reinforce the demand-shifting effect of off-peak discounts, particularly for low-fare products and for discounts shallower than approximately 47%.
item.dc:creator: Hannes Wallimann, Silvio Sticher, Christian Weibel

item.title: Fueling Inflation Risks: An Oil Shortage Scenario
item.description: arXiv:2611.12347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Central banks routinely use alternative scenarios to assess risks to the economic outlook, but these are usually generated from linear models that are unable to speak to the likelihood of extreme outcomes. We develop a nonlinear modeling framework that turns a narrative oil market scenario into a fully probabilistic assessment of the dynamics of oil and gasoline prices, aggregate inflation, and household inflation expectations. It combines an expert-based path for a tail event, a nonparametric model of the global oil market, and nonlinear Phillips curves for the energy, food, and core components of PCE inflation. We apply it in real time to quantify energy price and inflation risks of a severe oil shortage caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, modeled as a rapid drawdown of global petroleum inventories, using only information available in February 2026. Our analysis shows that once oil reserves hit rock bottom, oil and gasoline prices rise sharply, with risks tilted to the upside. Headline PCE inflation peaks near 4.8% in late 2026, and households expect inflation to rise by about 3 percentage points. Two years out, inflation is still highly likely to exceed the Fed's 2% target.
item.dc:creator: Christiane Baumeister, Todd Clark, Florian Huber

item.title: Fiscal Commitment and the Additionality of Philanthropy: Heterogeneous Donor Purposes in a Shared Public Budget
item.description: arXiv:2611.12459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Philanthropic donors often value different public services, while a budget authority allocates public spending across a shared portfolio. Policy frameworks frequently seek to ensure that private finance supplements rather than displaces public funding. We distinguish baseline additionality, which preserves pre-gift public funding, from portfolio preservation, which preserves a service's provision after all gifts are pooled under discretionary budgeting. A larger gift to one service raises the discretionary provision of every service and reduces the protection slack available to the others. This cross-donor fiscal externality yields an exact feasibility result: if a service's maximum permissible floor lies below its discretionary post-gift provision, every effective protection reform reduces that service relative to the portfolio reference, including full protection of its own appropriation. Conversely, a reform that expands at least one donor-backed service while preserving all others exists exactly when every maximum floor reaches the reference. The paper characterizes the complete preservation set and its welfare-maximizing element. Under logarithmic preferences, donation shares determine protectability, while heterogeneous donor valuations determine welfare incidence. Baseline additionality may therefore hold while a service loses fiscal benefits generated by other gifts.
item.dc:creator: Christian Jaag

item.title: That Time of the Year Again: Government Pay Revisions in the Aggregate Economy
item.description: arXiv:2611.12565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public pay is set by law in nominal terms, so inflation erodes its real value between legal acts until the government revises it. I model each revision as the choice of a forward-looking government, shaped by two costs that push in opposite directions. A fixed cost of acting makes revisions large and rare, whereas a convex cost of financing the increase at once makes them small and frequent. Through the budget, each revision also moves debt and the risk of fiscal stress under which the next one is made. In the documented pay decisions of eleven countries, pay set at discretion erodes against prices and private earnings and is restored in discrete steps, every cut was decided during market stress or an adjustment program, and court rulings drove a wedge between the cuts legislated, the cuts paid and the cuts that lasted. Estimated on the legal acts, the model reproduces the documented paths of pay in most countries when data and simulations are measured the same way. In Portugal's estimated model, the savings that the Treasury requires once spreads rise produce the cuts, the debt overhang holds pay down after the crisis, and a court that strikes cuts after they take effect invites cuts it will strike. Review of cuts before they took effect would have lowered the social cost of Portugal's crisis relative to review after the fact, and partial indexation would have paid in Bangladesh unless its automatic increases were costly to finance.
item.dc:creator: Faisal Quaiyyum

item.title: Winning Reviews, Losing Discovery? The Co-Evolutionary Game of AI Research and Peer Review
item.description: arXiv:2611.10791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous research systems can produce convincing manuscripts whose scientific value is difficult to verify, while automated reviewers can reward the appearance of completeness. We examine how this gap can become a self-reinforcing threat to the research community. In a two-population evolutionary game, authors choose between acceptance-oriented and exploratory research, and reviewers choose between proxy evaluation and careful assessment. Cheaper acceptance-oriented production can increase review pressure, making proxy assessment more attractive; proxy assessment can in turn strengthen the incentive to produce reviewer-compatible work. We derive conditions under which this feedback sustains a stable regime that rewards publication success while reducing the scientific value of accepted work. An analytical basin boundary explains why the same institutional rules can support either this regime or exploratory research with careful review. Numerical illustrations show how publication counts can conceal scientific loss, how faster adjustment can reinforce existing practices, and why partial reform may fail once the cycle is established. Careful audits and reviewer rewards can reverse the feedback, while temporary support can produce lasting recovery if it moves the community across the basin boundary. The model identifies a warning mechanism rather than forecasting a particular conference: a review system can remain operational and privately rewarding while becoming less effective at supporting discovery. Its institutional implication is to reward independently validated contributions and consequential checking, rather than accelerate paper production and scoring alone.
item.dc:creator: Hongze Liu, Mengru Wang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Yao Liu

item.title: Information Aggregation in Markets with Analysts, Experts, and Chatbots
item.description: arXiv:2411.01938v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study information aggregation when traders interpret public news, such as analyst reports, differently. This differential interpretation injects noise into equilibrium prices, compounding the informational bottleneck caused by noise traders. Next to analysts and experts, we consider the role of ``AI" chatbots, which (i) provide free financial advice and (ii) analyze traders' queries to learn about the asset's fundamental. Our model predicts that (i) chatbots aggregate information more efficiently than markets, (ii) increase trade volume, and (iii) enhance the informational content of prices. Ultimately, the AI platform extracts an absolute informational advantage over other market participants, highlighting a structural shift from information aggregation through market prices to ``AI" platforms.
item.dc:creator: Wolfgang Kuhle

item.title: Advancing AI Capabilities and Evolving Labor Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2507.08244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper examines how labor market outcomes have evolved across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from generative AI chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score that measures the share of each occupation's work that AI could perform at each capability stage, and link the change in exposure to the Current Population Survey from January 2023 through June 2026, using first-difference and fixed-effects designs at the occupation and individual level, with 2017 to 2022 as a placebo period. We find that occupations with larger increases in exposure show no change in employment or unemployment relative to occupations with comparable workforces. However, the composition of the workforce in these occupations changed. The number of workers under 30 decreased by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the change in exposure, and the decline is concentrated among workers without a college degree and builds gradually from 2023. It is not accompanied by higher unemployment among young workers who were already in these occupations, which suggests a decline in entry rather than an increase in exit. The decline is smaller when remote work is held fixed, but it remains. On the other hand, college graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time employment. Part-time work declined, weekly hours increased slightly, and the workforce in these occupations became older and more educated. In sum, the early effects of AI appear in the composition of the workforce rather than in the number of jobs.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Dominski, Tyler Boes, Yong Suk Lee

item.title: Wage-Setting Constraints and Firm Responses to Demand Shocks
item.description: arXiv:2512.19622v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates how institutional wage-setting constraints, such as a national minimum wage or collectively bargained wages, affect firm responses to demand shocks. We develop a framework to interpret heterogeneous shock responses that depend on the constraints firms face, and provide empirical evidence on the relevance of these constraints in shaping firm behavior in Portugal and Norway, two countries with different institutional settings. We discuss the implications of our findings for conventional measures of employer wage-setting power and rent-sharing.
item.dc:creator: Manudeep Bhuller, Lukas Delgado-Prieto, Santiago Hermo, Linnea Lorentzen

item.title: Jornada de trabalho, produtividade e informalidade: uma avaliacao quantitativa para o Brasil
item.description: arXiv:2602.03884v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper quantifies the total factor productivity (TFP) gain required to offset the short-run output loss associated with alternative weekly working-hour ceilings in Brazil. We combine moments from the 2024Q4 PNAD Cont\'inua with a static partial-equilibrium model in which formal and informal labor are imperfect substitutes, hourly efficiency depends on working hours, and formalization wedges govern the composition of employment. To represent reductions from 44 to 40 and 36 hours, we initially cap formal workers' usual hours at 44 as a baseline measurement assumption. The 40-hour alternative requires 1.53-1.57% higher TFP. Moving to 36 hours requires 6.52--8.38%, depending on the efficiency assumption below 40 hours; informality rises by 2.28-2.92 percentage points in the same counterfactual. Decompositions show that fewer physical formal hours account for the largest negative component of the output change. Comparison with Brazil's historical TFP path and welfare exercises suggests an important quantitative difference between moderate reforms and the 36-hour ceiling. Magnitudes depend on fatigue and baseline hours: retaining the observed usual-hours tail above 44 reduces the requirement at 40 hours to approximately 0.07%. The results motivate the assessment of gradual paths and transition instruments, without providing a causal estimate of the effects of a specific legislative proposal.
item.dc:creator: Victor Rangel, Fernando Barros Jr

item.title: The Process and Dynamics of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, 1969-2026
item.description: arXiv:2603.20767v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics has been awarded annually since 1969. Who wins the prize is a topic of much interest and tracks the whole course of the academic discipline over the last 57 years. Explaining who wins the prize in any given year is a complex process, which involves the subtle endogeneity of the choice of the field and the individual(s) who should be honoured. Citations, track records, networks of past winners, institutional factors along with field rotation and Economic Prize Committee composition may all play a role. A dynamic sample involving a changing stock of would-be candidates along with a moving flow -- both into and out of the sample -- add complexities to the modelling. We find robust evidence that the Nobel Prize rotates in a semi-regular way between the fields of economics. Later awards were for a small body of highly-cited work. Networks do not matter, but having a Nobel student or Nobel (older) co-author does. There is no evidence that the field specialisations of Committee members had an effect on either field or individual winner. The Committee's decisions changed after Lindbeck retired.
item.dc:creator: Peter J. Dolton, Richard S. J. Tol

item.title: Work that Counts, and Work that Doesn't: Reconciling Experimental and Observational Labor Supply Elasticities
item.description: arXiv:2605.29832v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Do workers behave the same in experiments as they do in real life? Combining a real-effort emoji-counting experiment with platform records, self-reported expectations and recalls, and smartphone screen-time logs, we compare how the same workers on Prolific respond to wage changes in the experiment and in their actual work. Our results reveal that workers' behavior in experiments is remarkably different from their behavior in real life. In the observational window, in fact, workers respond to expected wage changes just as they do in the experiment, but are much less responsive to unanticipated changes. However, once we condition on recall error in self-reports, we find that behavior in the two windows aligns. Recall error is then both a source of error in self-reported data and the result of a process of inattention that affects effort itself, as workers do not respond to unexpected wage changes that pass unnoticed.
item.dc:creator: Mattia Adamo, Michele Cantarella

item.title: Ever since Ellsberg
item.description: arXiv:2607.09355v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ellsberg's famous paradox challenged Savage's subjective expected utility theory (EUT) -- which reduces uncertainty to risk -- by suggesting an aversion toward ambiguity. We provide a revealed preference test of the full set of axioms underpinning subjective EUT under uncertainty and compare it to an analogous test of objective EUT under risk. We find that individual choices are as consistent with utility maximization and expected utility maximization under uncertainty as they are under risk. Nevertheless, there is greater empirical scope for non-EUT models under uncertainty than under risk, and the absolute and relative consistency of EUT and non-EUT models vary considerably across subjects.
item.dc:creator: Aluma Dembo, Shachar Kariv, Matthew Polisson, John K. -H. Quah

item.title: Large-Market Discipline in Combinatorial Double Auctions: No Recombination, Bundle Selection, and Complementarities
item.description: arXiv:2608.06134v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Licences can forbid assembling bundles from several sellers or splitting them among buyers, a restriction we call No Recombination. We study its welfare cost in a double auction as the number of traders on each side of the market grows. We ask whether that cost vanishes as a share of welfare, as the gain from misreporting does with a single good. With two goods and Gaussian shocks, consider the prices that would prevail under free recombination. As the market grows, the loss as a share of optimal welfare vanishes if and only if expected demand for the two-good bundle equals expected supply of whole bundles at those prices. Otherwise the loss persists. In our market, sellers can never gain by misreporting. With two goods, buyers who commit to bidding their values plus fixed margins misreport in symmetric equilibria by amounts that vanish as the market grows. Under these conditions, in large markets No Recombination outweighs strategic bidding as a source of loss.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos E. Zachariadis, Yongxin Yang

item.title: Whom Do AI Agents Serve? Role-Induced Sponsorship Bias in Decision Models and Generative LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2609.17989v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consumers increasingly delegate product search to AI shopping agents powered by generative large language models (LLMs) or non-generative decision models. Because retail platforms monetize through sponsored listings that consumers typically discount, we examine whether an AI agent's evaluation of sponsored listings depends on who delegates it. Across six LLMs and six decision models in Study 1, consumer-delegated agents penalize sponsored listings, whereas naming a booking platform as principal significantly attenuates this sponsorship penalty without instructions to favor advertisers. This sponsorship bias replicates across prompt wordings and LLM reasoning efforts and operates through reduced pre-choice skepticism in LLMs. In Study 2, attributing the paid placement to the platform amplifies sponsorship bias across both model families, and stricter disclosure wording ("Sponsored" vs. "Promoted") fails to eliminate it. In Study 3, prompt-level mitigation removes platform leniency but can over-correct the sponsorship penalty, whereas consumer-aligned fine-tuning eliminates sponsorship bias and better preserves baseline preferences.
item.dc:creator: Davood Wadi, Yu Ma

item.title: Organizational Lifespan as Commitment: The Case of Foundations
item.description: arXiv:2610.08447v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An organization's lifespan may commit future decision makers to continue, terminate, or retain discretion. We identify when each rule has value for philanthropic foundations. If the same aligned actor chooses investment and subsequent survival, discretion weakly dominates fixed rules; a commonly used investment comparison fails because it omits the option to invest enough to make continuation desirable in adverse states. With noncontractible organizational investment delegated to an earlier actor, however, perpetuity may improve incentives despite inefficient continuation in some states. The result survives an observable-investment extension. A finite terminal date is valuable under governance-induced overcontinuation, and its optimum reflects both direct operating benefits and investment incentives. We establish nonempty environments favoring each regime and distinguish institutional lifespan from payout policy, requirements to preserve the foundation's endowment capital, and the duration of grant commitments.
item.dc:creator: Christian Jaag

item.title: Climate change, sea level rise, and the agricultural revolution
item.description: arXiv:2610.37306v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We test various hypotheses for the invention and spread of agriculture: higher temperatures, increased seasonality, sea level rise, and technological progress on the extensive margin. We successfully replicate Matranga (QJE 2024). His seasonality hypothesis survives alternative data, estimators, competing hypotheses, and, for adoption but not invention, bootstrap clustering. Population density played a role in the invention of agriculture, while spatial diffusion was important for its spread. Sea level rise and climate change had a minor effect on the population density of the areas that first adopted agriculture. Extrapolating a logit model for the invention of agriculture, some now-submerged areas in the Persian Gulf, Mediterranean, and Yellow Sea were suitable for early agriculture. Over time, technological progress was the main factor in extending agriculture's extensive margin.
item.dc:creator: Ridhika Mishra, Richard S. J. Tol

item.title: What is Work For? Labor, Politics, and Meaning in the Age of AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.39375v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates the role of work in providing meaning, purpose, community, and other non-monetary benefits. Using an original cross-national survey of 8,234 working-age adults across the UK, US, Denmark, and India, I study the factors that motivate people in their work, with an eye toward the future AI economic transformation. I find that 81% of respondents report being satisfied with their job, and a majority across all four countries are strongly motivated by the non-monetary components of their employment. Using an original "Work Values" Index, I show that one third of working respondents are motivated intrinsically by their job--valuing their role for its own sake. Nearly one quarter are driven by social and community-related aspects of their employment, 17% by social status, and just over one quarter by the transactional financial benefits of their job. Although a majority of people would leave their role if offered their current salary as a guaranteed income, one fifth of workers would stay even if offered up to 120% of their salary. Intrinsically motivated workers were disproportionately likely to refuse a basic income at any substitution level. Groups attached to their job for non-monetary reasons were also more likely to pursue volunteering or work-like activities if they received guaranteed income substitution but could no longer perform their role. Crucially, these non-monetary work motivations are evenly distributed across the income distribution and between white- and blue-collar workers. I argue that these findings have implications for managing the AI transition, understanding attitudes to AI, and making sense of policy preferences. Guaranteeing a basic income may indeed be necessary for managing any future AI labor shock, yet it could ultimately fail to compensate workers for any loss of the non-monetary benefits they derive from work.
item.dc:creator: Julian Jacobs

item.title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
item.description: arXiv:2410.03897v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Using generative AI, we extract managers' economic expectations from over 120,000 corporate conference call transcripts. The resulting AI Economy Score predicts GDP growth, production, employment, and wages five or more quarters ahead, beyond survey forecasts and other existing measures. Industry- and firm-level scores capture sector- and firm-specific activity, and a composite of firm, industry, and macroeconomic expectations further improves forecasting power and horizon. Predictability concentrates among historically more accurate, less biased managers, consistent with an information rather than a noise channel. Managerial expectations thus offer incremental insights into economic activity, with implications for macro- and microeconomic decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Manish Jha, Jialin Qian, Michael Weber, Baozhong Yang

item.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2511.05766v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied as behavioral subjects (e.g., synthetic participants or users) and decision systems (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge), yet it remains unclear how observed cognitive biases relate to changes in model output probabilities. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, provides a useful test case. Prior research largely relies on generated responses, leaving distributional effects and input-field contributions less explored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis examining how numerical anchors shift distributions over candidate outputs, using alternative questions and anchor pairs alongside a positive control to reduce reliance on potentially memorized stimuli; (2) exact Banzhaf-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor contributions to log-probabilities; and (3) an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal predominantly positive behavioral anchoring effects, varying substantially across models. Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B achieve the highest ABSS rankings, whereas other models exhibit weaker behavioral-attributional alignment despite sometimes showing substantial behavioral shifts. Attributional effects also vary across prompts, indicating that behavioral anchoring does not necessarily imply stronger anchor-field contributions. These findings raise questions about LLM reliability as synthetic participants and potential vulnerabilities to numerical cues in automated evaluation and decision-making. More broadly, the framework connects behavioral science with explainable AI, particularly interpretability, and AI safety, providing a reproducible approach to investigating cognitive-bias-like effects in LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Felipe Valencia-Clavijo

item.title: Equilibrium Selection in Coordination Games with Planned Actions and Scouting
item.description: arXiv:2609.17608v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Stag Hunt games in which every action requires planning and preparation. Before players act, they observe noisy signals of their opponent's preparations and can revise their plans, which allows players to screen for cooperation. As screening becomes more precise and cheap, small trembles ensure that, in every equilibrium, play yields the payoff-dominant outcome with a probability that converges to one, even when the safe, low payoff equilibrium is risk dominant. Across scenarios, we emphasize that decomposing an action into (i) preparation and (ii) execution allows us to analyze simultaneous-move games in which players partially observe each other's contemporaneous actions.
item.dc:creator: Wolfgang Kuhle
